column2: Sensors and modules that stay powered. Power the sensor from a GPIO pin or through a transistor so it can be switched off during sleep, if its current is small.
A voltage divider for reading the battery: 20 kΩ + 10 kΩ on 8.4 V draws 0.28 mA continuously. Use larger resistors or switch it off during sleep.

The ESP32 datasheet says about 10 µA in deep sleep, but one measurement of an ESP32-DevKitC V4 board found about 3.8 mA in deep sleep: nearly 400 times more. The cause was the power LED, the AMS1117 regulator and the USB chip on that board, not the ESP32. For battery projects, choose a board designed to save power, or measure the current yourself.
Two boards are both active for 5 seconds every 10 minutes. Board A sleeps at 0.01 mA, board B sleeps at 5 mA. Which matters most for the difference in battery life?
The sleep current. The board sleeps almost 99% of the time, so 5 mA while asleep matters far more than 120 mA for 5 seconds.
A 1000 mAh battery and an average current of 2 mA. Roughly how long?
1000 / 2 = 500 hours, times 0.7 ≈ 350 hours, about two weeks.
Calculating and measuring consumption
Resistors and voltage dividers
The simplest component, and the basis of nearly every analog sensor reading.

A resistor limits current (for example for an LED) or divides voltage. Its value is written with color bands: the first two or three bands are digits, then the multiplier, then the tolerance (how far the real value may be off). The small resistors in a kit are usually 1/4 W: enough for signals and LEDs, not for large currents.
Resistor color band reader
Hold the resistor with the tolerance band on the right (gold or silver, or on a 5-band resistor usually a brown one set slightly apart), then read from the left.
Voltage divider

Two resistors in series divide the voltage according to their ratio. The midpoint gives a smaller voltage. The most common uses: lowering a 5 V signal to a 3.3 V pin (for example the echo of an HC-SR04 distance sensor), and reading a battery voltage higher than 3.3 V with an ADC.
A 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ divider lowers 5 V to 3.33 V.
Voltage divider calculator
Potentiometers and resistive sensors

A potentiometer is a voltage divider you can turn: the middle leg gives the voltage between the two outer legs. Many sensors work the same way: an LDR (resistance changes with light) and a thermistor (changes with temperature) are placed in series with a fixed resistor, and the midpoint is read by the ADC.

The HC-SR04 distance sensor module works at 5 V and outputs a 5 V echo signal. On an Arduino Uno (5 V) that is fine directly. On an ESP32 or Pico (3.3 V), the echo goes through a 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ divider first, because 3.3 V pins are not designed for 5 V.
A 4-band resistor red-red-brown-gold. What is its value?
You want to read a battery up to 8.4 V with an ADC that maxes out around 3.1 V. Which divider suits?
For example 20 kΩ (top) and 10 kΩ (bottom): 8.4 × 10 / 30 = 2.8 V. The code then multiplies the result by 3.
An LDR and a 10 kΩ resistor are set up as a divider. If the room gets brighter, the LDR resistance drops. What happens to the midpoint voltage if the LDR is in the top position (R1)?
It rises. R1 gets smaller, so R2's share of the total gets larger.
Resistors and dividers
Capacitors and noise
Why almost every IC has a small capacitor next to it.
A capacitor stores charge briefly and releases it quickly. In microcontroller projects it has two main jobs:
Decoupling (100 nF) near the power pins of every IC or module: absorbs fast noise and gives momentary current when the chip changes state. Most modules already carry one.

Buffering (10-1000 µF) at the power entry point, especially near motors, servos, relays, LED strips or radio modules: releases charge when the load suddenly draws current, so the voltage does not dip.
A capacitor covers the momentary shortfall near the load, before the distant source can catch up.
Electrolytics are polarized and large in value; ceramics are non-polarized and small in value.
Ceramic codes

The long leg (+) goes to the positive side, the striped side (−) to GND. Use a capacitor whose rated voltage is clearly above the working voltage, for example 10 V or 16 V for a 5 V rail. A reversed capacitor can get hot, leak, swell or burst.
Noise: where it comes from and how to dampen it
Noise sources: motors (sparking at the brushes), relays and solenoids when switched off, switching converters, and long wires that pick up interference from their surroundings.
Separate the power paths of big loads from the chip's power path, then join the GNDs at a single point.
Keep signal wires as short as possible, and away from motor wires. A long sensor wire can be twisted together with its GND wire.
A small capacitor (100 nF) across a DC motor's terminals dampens the sparking from its brushes.
In code: average several ADC readings, and ignore changes too fast to make sense.

A servo moves randomly, so the 470 µF capacitor on its power line is removed to test. Nothing changes. That makes sense: a capacitor dampens spikes, but it cannot replace a broken GND, a loose connection, or a servo hitting its travel limit. A capacitor is not a cure for every strange symptom.
A ceramic capacitor marked 103. What is its value?
A radio module often resets when it sends data. Where should the buffer capacitor be placed?
As close as possible to that module's power pins (VCC to GND), with the correct polarity.
Can a 6.3 V electrolytic capacitor be used on a 5 V rail?
It can work, but it is marginal. 10 V or 16 V is safer, because the voltage can briefly rise and a capacitor near its limit fails sooner.
Identifying capacitors
Diodes and LEDs
Components that pass current in only one direction.

A diode passes current in only one direction: from anode to cathode (the striped side). When conducting, the diode "uses" about 0.6-0.7 V (silicon diodes such as 1N4007, 1N4148) or about 0.2-0.4 V (Schottky diodes).
Forward: the valve opens. Reverse: the valve is pressed against its seat and nothing flows.
Three common uses:
Polarity protection: a series diode in the power input prevents damage when a battery or adapter is connected backwards, at the cost of a small voltage drop.
Flyback diode: placed across a relay or motor coil (stripe to +) to absorb the voltage kick when the coil is switched off. See Chapter 9.
Source isolation: two sources joined through diodes so current cannot flow back from one into the other.
An LED is a diode that lights up. The long leg = anode (+). An LED always needs a resistor to limit the current:
LED color
Approximate Vf
Yellow, ordinary green
Blue, white, bright green
LED resistor calculator

A white LED connected from a 3.3 V pin with a 220 Ω resistor glows very dimly. Its Vf is about 3.1 V, so the resistor carries only 0.2 V: the current is about 1 mA. For white or blue LEDs, a 3.3 V source leaves almost no room. Use a smaller resistor (for example 47-68 Ω) or a 5 V source through a transistor.
A blue LED (Vf 3.0 V) on 5 V at 10 mA. What resistor?
(5 − 3) / 0.010 = 200 Ω. Use the nearest standard value above it: 220 Ω.
An LED is connected backwards with a resistor on 3.3 V. What happens?
It does not light, because the diode blocks reverse current. At a voltage this low the LED is not damaged.
A 1N4007 diode is placed in series as polarity protection on a 5 V line. What voltage reaches the board?
About 5 − 0.7 = 4.3 V. For a board that needs exactly 5 V, use a Schottky diode or a MOSFET as the protection.

Transistors, MOSFETs and relays
How a small pin controls a big load without burning up.

A microcontroller pin can supply only a small current (Chapter 10). To switch on something bigger (a relay, a loud buzzer, an LED strip, a motor, a pump), the pin just gives the command, and another component connects the load to its own power source.
A small flow opens the way for a large flow.
The actual circuit: the load current flows from +5 V through the coil and transistor to GND. The pin only controls the base.
Good for
Things to watch
NPN transistor (BC547, 2N2222)
loads up to about 100-500 mA: relays, buzzers, small LEDs
1 kΩ base resistor from the pin; emitter to GND; load between + and the collector
Logic-level MOSFET (AO3400, IRLZ44N)
big loads: LED strips, motors, pumps
choose one that turns fully on at your pin's voltage (3.3 V); gate resistor about 100-220 Ω, and 10 kΩ from gate to GND
Relay module
switches another, electrically separate load on and off
many modules are active LOW; a 5 V module is not necessarily triggered reliably by a 3.3 V signal
Motor driver (L298N, TB6612, DRV8833)
DC motor in both directions
direction and speed from pins; motor power from its own source

When the current in a relay, solenoid or motor coil is suddenly cut, the coil kicks out a high reverse voltage. Without a diode (for example 1N4007, stripe to +), that kick can damage the transistor or reset the microcontroller. A good relay module already has one fitted.

The IRF520 MOSFET module that is popular in online shops is often used with an ESP32, and the result is a load that only glows dimly or a MOSFET that gets hot. The IRF520 datasheet gives a gate threshold voltage of 2-4 V, and its low on-resistance is only reached with 10 V on the gate. With 3.3 V it can barely turn on, and even with 5 V it does not turn fully on. Choose a MOSFET labeled logic-level whose datasheet gives the on-resistance at 2.5-4.5 V.
A 5 V relay draws 80 mA. Can its coil be connected straight to an ESP32 pin?
No. The current is far above what the pin can supply, and the coil's kick can damage the pin. Use a transistor and a flyback diode, or a relay module.
A relay module turns on when the pin is LOW and off when the pin is HIGH. Why?
The module is active LOW. In the code, invert the logic: LOW = on, HIGH = off.
Why is there a 10 kΩ resistor from the MOSFET gate to GND?
So the gate does not float while the pin is not yet configured (for example during boot), which keeps the load from switching on by itself.
Switching a load through a transistor
Microcontroller pins
What may and may not be connected to a pin, and why a pin can read random numbers.
3.3 V and 5 V logic
A digital signal has only two states: HIGH and LOW, always relative to GND. The HIGH voltage depends on the board.
Pin limits (datasheet)
Arduino Uno (ATmega328P)
absolute maximum 40 mA per pin; 200 mA total on VCC
inputs up to about 3.6 V; about 40 mA at maximum drive
ESP8266, Raspberry Pi Pico
inputs are not designed for 5 V
ESP8266 has one ADC pin; Pico 12 bit

The absolute maximum numbers are the limit before damage, not working numbers. Stay well below them: a single 10 mA LED is no problem, motors and relays must go through a transistor (Chapter 9). A 5 V signal into a 3.3 V board must be lowered with a voltage divider or a level shifter. Conversely, a 3.3 V signal into a 5 V module is often read as HIGH, but not always.
Floating inputs and pull-ups

An input pin that is not connected to anything reads HIGH and LOW at random, exactly like the module without a shared GND in Chapter 2. For a button, use a pull-up resistor (to 3.3 V) or a pull-down (to GND), so the pin always has a clear state.
The pull-up holds the pin HIGH; the button pulls it LOW when pressed.
pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP) turns on the pull-up inside the chip (about 45 kΩ on the ESP32), so the external resistor can be left out.
Bouncing: a button's contacts bounce for a few milliseconds when pressed, so one press can be read several times. Ignore changes within 20-50 ms after the first change (debounce in the code).
ADC: reading voltage

The ADC turns voltage into a number. The formula is roughly voltage = number / max_number × reference_voltage. The ESP32 ADC is less accurate near 0 V and near its upper limit, so for measurements that need to be exact, calibrate against a multimeter or use an external ADC (for example the ADS1115). A voltage above its limit must first be lowered with a divider (Chapter 6).
